quote: I talked to somebody, like, maybe two years ago, and I just kinda regret not doing it then, now.
stewart_read: The customer hands the rep a strong emotional anchor — regret over a missed opportunity — but the rep's reply pivots straight to tax-credit mechanics rather than reflecting the regret back as urgency ('let's make sure you don't have that same regret again').
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the tax-credit question as the more pressing informational need and addressed it first, intending to return to the regret theme later — but no later line references it again.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to name the emotional hook explicitly when it surfaces — a one-line callback ('let's not let this be the same story as two years ago') costs nothing and reinforces motivation heading into button-up.

quote: Well, I mean, will you be able to send me some program information in the meantime?
stewart_read: Customer's request for material before the appointment is a soft hedge on commitment. The rep's response two lines later held the harder line (no design without a scheduled appointment) before offering a softer concession of 'basics' — a disciplined split between the hard rule and a reasonable accommodation.
alternative_hypothesis: A stricter reading might call the 'basics' email offer a partial cave on the hard rule, but the rep explicitly protected the design itself, which is the actual hard-rule content.
coaching_implication: Credit the rep for holding the design-withholding line; note the appointment is still conditional in the customer's own words ('tentatively... I'll let you know if that doesn't work'), so the handoff should flag it as fragile.

quote: I don't have anything that I would be able to send, just because we don't even build a design without having anything scheduled beforehand.
stewart_read: This is a clean strategy match against the schema's hard rule — the rep does not cave and does not promise to send the actual design, instead redirecting to a scheduled appointment as the gate.
coaching_implication: Positive moment to reinforce with the rep directly — this is the correct pattern for this objection and can be used as their own example of holding the line.

quote: My usage is gone way up, wasn't it?
stewart_read: The customer surfaces a striking self-observed data point (usage nearly doubling) unprompted. The rep asks a reasonable follow-up about cause ('Did anything change, like new appliances?') but the exchange settles on a generic weather explanation rather than flipping the number into urgency against the utility.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's appliance/weather questions show real engagement with the number rather than silent filing — this is a partial capture-and-acknowledge, not a full non-engagement.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to close this loop with an explicit flip line once the number is confirmed — e.g., tying the near-doubled usage directly to the appointment's purpose — since the acknowledgment stopped short of that reframe.

quote: Sweet. Well, thank you so much for grabbing that, Zachary. What I'll do is we'll get this uploaded. We'll tentatively schedule you for Monday at 03:30.
stewart_read: The close never uses the 'is that fair?' handshake, never states the one-hour block, and never delivers the no-driving/computer instruction — it closes on 'tentatively schedule' language with no locking mechanic.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's fallback-call plan ('we'll call Monday morning to make sure that time still works') could be read as a deliberate substitute for a hard lock, appropriate given the customer's own hedging — but this is a workaround for fragility, not the schema's actual button-up protocol.
coaching_implication: Walk the rep through the full button_up checklist (hour block, no-driving/computer, handshake) — even on a hedging customer, these elements can still be stated as the standard and would strengthen show-rate odds.
